body:
What is additive manufacturing?

Additive manufacturing (AM), commonly called 3D printing, is a manufacturing method in which a physical object is built by adding material according to a digital design. In many processes, the object is formed through successive layers of material.

For example, a computer can contain a digital model of a small plastic gear. A 3D printer follows instructions derived from that model and gradually builds the gear. The final object has length, breadth and height, unlike the flat output of an ordinary paper printer.

Additive manufacturing: The production of a physical 3-dimensional object by adding material, generally layer by layer, according to a digital model.

How additive manufacturing differs from conventional methods

Manufacturing methods can be distinguished by what happens to the starting material.

MethodBasic principleSimple example
Additive manufacturingMaterial is added to build the required shape.Printing a plastic component in successive layers.
Subtractive manufacturingUnwanted material is removed from a larger piece.Cutting or drilling a metal block to obtain a machine part.
Formative manufacturingMaterial is shaped, often using a mould or applied force.Making a plastic article by injection moulding.

A computer-controlled machine is not necessarily a 3D printer. A computer numerical control (CNC) machine that removes metal is performing subtractive manufacturing, even though its movements are digitally controlled.

How a digital model becomes a physical object

  1. Prepare a digital model: A 3-dimensional design is created using computer-aided design (CAD) software or obtained from a suitable digital scan.
  2. Divide the model into layers: Slicing software converts the model into instructions that describe how the machine should build it.
  3. Prepare the material: The selected process may use plastic filament, liquid resin, powder, wire or another suitable feedstock.
  4. Build the object: The machine adds material in the required locations. Depending on the process, the material may be deposited, melted, bonded or hardened by light.
  5. Finish the object: The completed part may need cleaning, removal of temporary supports, curing, heat treatment or surface finishing.

Why the method is important

Traditional production may require a separate mould or cutting tool for a particular shape. In many additive manufacturing processes, a change in the digital model is sufficient to begin producing a different design, although machine preparation and testing may still be necessary.

This makes additive manufacturing useful for rapid prototyping, in which a model or sample is produced to check the shape, fit or function of a product before large-scale production begins. It is also useful when a small number of customised parts is required.

The method offers greater freedom to create certain complex shapes, such as internal passages, lightweight structures and parts combining features that would otherwise require assembly. However, not every shape or material can be printed successfully, and printed components may require substantial finishing and quality checks.

3D printing is not the same as nanotechnology. Additive manufacturing describes how an object is made. Nanotechnology concerns materials and structures at the nanometre scale. Some advanced manufacturing methods may use nanomaterials, but ordinary 3D printing does not become nanotechnology merely because it is computer-controlled.

Prelims focus

  • Additive manufacturing builds an object by adding material.
  • Subtractive manufacturing removes unwanted material.
  • CAD provides the digital model; slicing converts it into manufacturing instructions.
  • Rapid prototyping is a major application of additive manufacturing.
  • Post-processing may still be necessary after printing.
  • Trap: Digital control alone does not make a manufacturing process additive.

[Sources: ISO, ISO/ASTM 52900:2021, Additive Manufacturing—General Principles—Fundamentals and Vocabulary, abstract and general principles, confirmed in 2025, consulted 14 November 2026; Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, National Strategy for Additive Manufacturing, February 2022, as explained in Press Information Bureau, Additive Manufacturing in India, sections Understanding Additive Manufacturing Technology and Additive Manufacturing Materials, 7 October 2026, consulted 14 November 2026; NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8, chapter Industries, printed pp. 50–52.]

title: Additive Manufacturing: The Basic Principle of 3D Printing

body:
Why there are different 3D-printing processes

All additive manufacturing processes build an object through the addition of material, but they do not use the same material form or method of joining it. Some deposit molten plastic; others harden a liquid resin, fuse powder, apply a binding liquid or join sheets.

The international terminology standard ISO/ASTM 52900:2021 recognises 7 broad categories of additive manufacturing processes. These are categories rather than 7 individual machine models. Different commercial technologies can belong to the same category.

The 7 categories and their working principles

Process categoryHow it worksTypical material
Material extrusionMaterial is forced through a nozzle and deposited in the required places.Thermoplastic filament or other extrudable material.
Vat photopolymerizationSelected regions of liquid photosensitive resin are hardened by light.Liquid photopolymer resin.
Powder bed fusionThermal energy selectively joins regions of a powder bed.Metal or polymer powder.
Binder jettingA liquid binding agent is deposited to join powder particles.Metal, ceramic or other suitable powder.
Material jettingSmall droplets of build material are deposited and then solidified.Photopolymer resin or wax.
Directed energy depositionFocused energy melts material as it is supplied to the build location.Usually metal powder or wire.
Sheet laminationSuccessive sheets are bonded together and shaped to form an object.Paper, polymer sheets or suitable metal sheets.

Important differences between similar processes

Material extrusion and vat photopolymerization

In common filament-based 3D printing, a plastic filament is heated and deposited through a nozzle. The deposited material cools and retains its shape. This belongs to material extrusion. The terms fused deposition modelling (FDM) and fused filament fabrication (FFF) are associated with this family.

In vat photopolymerization, the starting material is a photosensitive liquid. Light hardens selected portions to form the object. Stereolithography (SLA) is a well-known example. A vat-resin printer is therefore not a filament-extrusion printer.

Powder bed fusion and binder jetting

Both processes can begin with a bed of powder, but their joining mechanisms differ. Powder bed fusion uses heat to fuse selected powder regions. Binder jetting deposits a liquid binding agent onto selected powder regions. Some binder-jetted metal components subsequently require heating and densification to obtain useful strength.

Material jetting and binder jetting

These terms are easily confused. In material jetting, the deposited droplets become part of the object. In binder jetting, the deposited liquid principally serves to bind a separate powder material.

Directed energy deposition and sheet lamination

Directed energy deposition supplies material and focused energy together, usually to deposit metal on a surface. It can be useful for certain metal-part repairs and additions. Sheet lamination joins pre-existing sheets; it is not based on melting powder in a bed.

The joining mechanism is the key distinction. A nozzle depositing material suggests extrusion; light hardening a liquid in a vat suggests photopolymerization; heat fusing a powder bed suggests powder bed fusion; and liquid binder joining powder suggests binder jetting.

Prelims focus

  • ISO/ASTM 52900 identifies 7 broad additive manufacturing process categories.
  • FDM/FFF belongs to material extrusion.
  • SLA belongs to vat photopolymerization.
  • Powder bed fusion uses thermal energy to join powder.
  • Binder jetting uses a binding agent rather than relying on direct powder fusion during deposition.
  • Trap: Material jetting and binder jetting do not deposit the same type of material for the same purpose.

[Sources: ISO, ISO/ASTM 52900:2021, section 3.2, Process Categories, consulted 14 November 2026; National Institute of Standards and Technology, Additive Manufacturing Technologies, sections Powder Bed Fusion, Directed Energy Deposition, Material Extrusion, Vat Photopolymerization, Binder Jetting and Material Jetting, updated 15 April 2025, consulted 14 November 2026; Loughborough University, Additive Manufacturing Research Group, The 7 Categories of Additive Manufacturing, section Sheet Lamination, consulted 14 November 2026.]

title: The 7 Main Additive Manufacturing Processes

body:
Why material selection matters

The material used in additive manufacturing affects how a component is produced and how it performs. A material suitable for a classroom model may be unsuitable for a medical implant or an aircraft component.

Important properties include strength, hardness, flexibility, heat resistance, corrosion resistance, weight and, for medical applications, biocompatibility. Biocompatibility means that a material is suitable for its intended interaction with the human body.

Polymers: commonly used printing materials

A polymer consists of many repeating molecular units joined together. Plastics are an important group of polymer materials. Their ease of shaping makes many of them suitable for 3D printing.

Thermoplastics

Thermoplastics soften when heated and harden when cooled. This behaviour is useful in material-extrusion printing. Common examples include:

  • PLA (polylactic acid): Commonly used for models and prototypes because it is relatively easy to print. Its heat resistance is limited compared with some engineering plastics.
  • ABS (acrylonitrile butadiene styrene): Used for functional plastic components where toughness and heat resistance are useful. Printing generally requires greater temperature control than PLA.
  • Nylon: A family of polymers valued for toughness and wear resistance in suitable applications.
  • PETG: A modified polyester used for components requiring a useful combination of toughness and ease of printing.

Thermoplastics should not be confused with thermosetting materials, which form structures that cannot simply be remelted and reshaped in the same manner after curing. Many light-cured 3D-printing resins fall into the latter category.

Photosensitive resins

A photopolymer resin contains materials that harden through a light-induced chemical reaction. Such resins are used in vat photopolymerization and some material-jetting processes. They are useful for intricate models and fine details, but handling, curing and suitability for final use require attention.

Metals, ceramics and composites

Material groupImportant property or featureIllustrative application
Stainless steel and other metal alloysUseful mechanical strength; selected alloys resist corrosion.Industrial components and tooling.
Titanium alloysUseful combination of strength, low weight and corrosion resistance.Certain aerospace and medical components.
CeramicsMay offer hardness, heat resistance or biological compatibility, depending on composition.Technical parts and selected dental applications.
CompositesCombine constituent materials to obtain desired properties.Lightweight structural or functional parts.

Composites contain 2 or more different constituent materials. For example, reinforcing fibres may be combined with a polymer to improve particular properties. The resulting material's performance depends on the constituents, their proportions and their arrangement.

Material form and process compatibility

The same general material family may be supplied in different forms. Plastic may be supplied as a filament, pellet or powder; metals may be supplied as powder or wire. A printer designed for one feedstock cannot automatically use every other form.

Material choice must also match the final use. A plastic prototype can demonstrate whether a component fits into an assembly, but that does not establish that the same plastic will be suitable for high temperatures or heavy mechanical loads.

Not every 3D-printing resin is medically safe, and not every printable metal component is suitable for aerospace use. Material suitability depends on the specific grade, manufacturing process, finishing and required testing.

Prelims focus

  • PLA, ABS, nylon and PETG are polymer materials used in suitable 3D-printing processes.
  • Thermoplastics can soften on heating and harden on cooling.
  • Photopolymer resins harden through a light-induced reaction.
  • Titanium alloys are valued in selected applications for their strength-to-weight characteristics.
  • Metal powders and metal wires are different feedstock forms.
  • Trap: The presence of a familiar material name does not establish the safety or qualification of the finished part.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 8, chapter Synthetic Fibres and Plastics, printed pp. 32–37; NCERT, Science, Class 9, chapter Is Matter Around Us Pure?, printed pp. 14–16, discussion of mixtures and alloys; National Institute of Standards and Technology, Additive Manufacturing Technologies, sections Materials and Technologies, updated 15 April 2025, consulted 14 November 2026; Press Information Bureau, Additive Manufacturing in India, section Additive Manufacturing Materials, 7 October 2026, consulted 14 November 2026.]
